Question 39. Nested tokenization state

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual debugging problem

An outer strtok loop splits a line into semicolon-separated records. Inside it, another strtok loop splits the current record into comma-separated fields. Why can the next outer iteration fail to continue its original line, and what design avoids the dependency?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The inner call begins a new tokenization sequence and replaces the saved continuation state used by strtok. A subsequent outer call with null input resumes that most recently saved sequence rather than automatically remembering the outer one. The text buffers themselves being distinct does not supply separate continuation objects. Use a parser with explicit state for each nesting level, or a documented reentrant platform API with distinct state variables. A span parser can also preserve both the source bytes and independent cursor positions. This is a state-management defect, not just a delimiter spelling mistake.

Question 40. Line input at exact capacity

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original stream-boundary problem

With char b[5], a successful fgets(b,5,stdin) reads from a stream beginning with abcd\n. State the buffer and what remains in the stream. Can absence of newline in the buffer alone prove EOF?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The call can store at most four input bytes before its added zero, so the buffer becomes a b c d 0. The newline remains unread in the stream because capacity is exhausted first. No newline in the buffer therefore does not prove EOF; this call stopped because of its byte limit. A following call can read the newline. The program must define whether to consume the remainder of a line or handle it in chunks. Blindly replacing b[strlen(b)-1] would wrongly discard the real final d.

Question 41. Removing newline without losing data

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original input-contract problem

For successful ordinary-text fgets results "ab\n", "ab", and "", evaluate the strategy p=strchr(b,'\n'); if(p) *p=0;. Contrast with always writing b[strlen(b)-1]=0.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The guarded search changes ab followed by newline into ab. It leaves ab without newline unchanged and also leaves the valid empty string unchanged. The blind last-byte strategy happens to remove newline in the first case, incorrectly removes b in the second, and subtracts one from zero in the third, producing an invalid index. An empty successful string view can arise when input contains an embedded zero; it is not a reason to assume a newline exists. The guarded operation conditions mutation on the actual byte being removed.

Question 42. Formatted input width

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original library distinction

An eight-byte writable array is used with %8s, %7s, and %7c. Which successful conversion fits and creates a string? Explain the storage requirement and whitespace behavior.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

%8s can read eight content bytes and append a ninth zero, so it is unsafe for an eight-byte array on a maximum-width token. %7s reads at most seven content bytes, adds zero, fits, skips leading whitespace, and stops at whitespace. %7c reads seven character bytes when successful, including whitespace, and does not append zero. It fits as raw character input but does not itself establish a string. Check the return count and establish termination separately when using %c. Width has conversion-specific meaning.

Question 43. Formatting and would-have length

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original return-value calculation

Assume ASCII and no encoding error. Evaluate snprintf(b,5,"%s-%d","abcd",12): actual stored string, return value, truncation status, and minimum capacity for the complete result.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The untruncated formatted content is abcd-12, seven bytes. With capacity 5, only four content bytes fit before zero, so the stored string is abcd. The return is 7, the required content length, not the number actually stored. Since 7≥5, truncation occurred. Complete storage requires 8 bytes including zero. A negative return would be a distinct error status and should be handled before conversion to size_t for a capacity comparison. The function does not allocate the missing space.

Question 44. The special zero-size formatting query

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original contract distinction

Why can snprintf(NULL,0,"%s","cat") be used as a size query, whereas memcmp(NULL,NULL,0) must not be justified by “zero bytes are accessed” under ISO C17's string-library conventions?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

snprintf explicitly permits a null destination when its size is zero and writes nothing, so this call returns 3 under successful formatting. The string-library conventions in Section 7.24 instead require valid pointer arguments even for zero counts unless an individual description states an exception. A programmer cannot infer permission for memcmp solely from an implementation that happens to avoid a load. Both contracts are specified independently of generated machine code. A custom function may explicitly accept null for an empty range, but that policy must be stated rather than transferred to a library call.

Question 45. Character classification domain

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original signed-char safety problem

Why is isalpha(s[i]) unsafe when a stored byte promotes to a negative integer other than EOF? Give the corrected expression and explain why casting the return value instead would not repair the call.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The classification function's argument must be EOF or representable as unsigned char. A negative promoted plain-char byte outside that domain violates the contract. isalpha((unsigned char)s[i]) converts the stored byte into its nonnegative unsigned representation before integer promotion, satisfying the domain. Casting the returned truth value occurs after the invalid call and cannot repair its precondition. If the original value came directly from getchar, retain it as int, check for EOF, and only then classify the character. Locale still affects which valid bytes are classified as letters.

Question 46. Numeric conversion needs a status

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original parser reasoning

Compare strtol processing of "0", " -12x", and "xyz" in base ten. Ignore range overflow for these small inputs. State values, end-pointer locations, and which inputs satisfy a whole-string integer policy allowing leading whitespace but no trailing bytes.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

0 converts to value 0 and leaves the end pointer at its terminating zero, so it satisfies the policy. The second input converts to -12 after skipping leading spaces and stops at x; its trailing nonzero byte violates the whole-string policy. xyz performs no conversion, returns 0, and leaves the end pointer equal to the original start. It therefore fails despite sharing the numerical result of the valid input 0. For general inputs also reset and inspect errno for range errors. The value alone is not a complete parse result.

Question 47. UTF-8 bytes and displayed characters

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original representation problem

Under UTF-8, compare precomposed U+00E9 with the sequence U+0065 U+0301. Give byte counts, code-point counts, and typical grapheme counts. Which count does strlen return, and is byte reversal a valid text reversal?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

U+00E9 encodes in two bytes and is one code point. U+0065 occupies one byte and U+0301 two, so their sequence occupies three bytes and contains two code points. Both commonly display as one grapheme cluster. Provided each byte sequence is terminated, strlen returns 2 and 3. Reversing the bytes can break UTF-8 continuation-byte structure. Even reversing code points is not generally grapheme-safe because it may separate the combining mark from its base. A text operation must state its counting and segmentation unit; ordinary byte algorithms do not solve that problem automatically.

Question 48. Rows versus pointer tables

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original storage calculation

Assume pointers occupy eight bytes. Compare char rows[3][8] and const char *p[3]={"a","bb","ccc"}: size of each outer object, total bytes in the three separately counted literals, and permitted reassignment.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The row object occupies 3·8=24 bytes. The pointer table also occupies 3·8=24 bytes on this implementation, but this numerical coincidence hides different structure. Separately counting the three literal arrays uses (1+1)+(2+1)+(3+1)=9 bytes; compiler merging can affect physical placement, so this is a representation count under the stated separate-count policy. p[0]=p[1] reassigns a pointer and is permitted. rows[0]=rows[1] is invalid whole-array assignment. Writable row bytes may be changed; the literal contents must not be modified.

Question 49. Arguments and their final sentinel

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original pointer-level distinction

Suppose argc==3 and argv points to "tool", "", and "ab", followed by a null pointer. Determine the sum of argument lengths, content-plus-terminator storage, and whether argv[1] and argv[3] denote the same kind of empty input.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The lengths are 4, 0, and 2, summing to 6 content bytes. Counting their three terminating zeros adds three, yielding nine character bytes, excluding the pointer table. argv[1] points to a valid one-byte empty-string representation and may be passed to strlen, returning zero. argv[3] is the null pointer sentinel and must not be dereferenced or passed to strlen. Four pointer entries are needed to include that sentinel; the extra pointer is not an extra argument string. The distinction is between levels of representation.

Question 50. Quadratic repeated concatenation

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original exact-sum problem

Append k strings of length r≥1 to an empty destination using a scalar strcat that scans the destination through zero and copies the source through zero each time. Derive the total byte inspections in those two phases and evaluate k=5,r=3.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Before append j for j=0,…,k−1, existing length is jr, so destination scanning inspects jr+1 bytes. Source copying reads r+1 bytes. Total inspections are ∑j=0k−1(jr+r+2)=rk(k−1)/2+kr+2k. For five pieces of length three, this is 30+15+10=55. The source phase also writes k(r+1)=20 bytes, a separate operation count. Maintaining an end pointer removes repeated prefix scans but does not remove the content copies or necessary termination policy.

Question 51. Geometric buffer growth

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original amortized-cost derivation

A buffer starts with capacity 1 and doubles until capacity 2h. At each growth it copies its entire old capacity. Sum the copied bytes and compare with final capacity. Does this imply every append is constant time?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Old capacities copied are 1,2,4,…,2h−1. Their sum is 2h−1, strictly less than the final capacity. Across a sequence of enough appends to reach that size, total growth copying is linear in the final capacity, supporting constant amortized growth cost per appended byte under the model. The last individual growth copies 2h−1 bytes and is linear, so worst-case single-append time is not constant. Overflow, allocation failure, and content length plus terminator still require checks; the geometric sum only analyzes successful modeled growth.

Question 52. Reallocation and ownership

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original lifetime proof obligation

Explain why p=realloc(p,newcap) risks losing owned storage when allocation fails. Give the correct ownership transition and clarify whether an old alias may still be used after a successful reallocation that returns an equal numerical address.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For a positive requested size, failure returns null while leaving the original allocation intact. Direct assignment overwrites the sole owning pointer, potentially leaking that allocation. Store the result in a temporary, test it, and update the owner only on success. On successful reallocation, the old allocation's lifetime ends and the returned pointer designates the new allocation; old aliases must not be used even if the displayed address happens to be unchanged. Recompute interior pointers from the new base and validated offsets. Ownership reasoning follows lifetime, not just address numerals.

Question 53. Count abstract string values

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original geometric-series problem

A capacity-5 buffer stores strings over three allowed nonzero bytes. How many distinct string values can it represent? Why is 35 not the correct answer?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

At least one slot must hold the terminator, so content lengths range from 0 through 4. For each length j, there are 3j values. The total is 1+3+9+27+81=121, equivalently (35−1)/(3−1). The expression 35 counts length-5 content sequences, none of which fits with its terminator in capacity 5. Bytes after an earlier terminator do not create additional string values. The empty string contributes exactly one value and must not be omitted.

Question 54. Count terminated storage states

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original first-zero partition

Each byte of a capacity-4 array independently takes one of zero and two nonzero values. Count complete array states containing a zero, and count states whose first zero is at index 2. Compare with the number of abstract values.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There are 34=81 complete states. The 24=16 states with no zero are not terminated, leaving 65 terminated states. To put the first zero at index 2, the first two bytes must be nonzero (four choices), index 2 must be zero (one choice), and the final byte is unrestricted (three choices), giving 12. Abstract values number 1+2+4+8=15. Many of the 65 terminated states represent the same value because bytes after the first zero may vary freely.

Question 55. Probability of finding a terminator

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original probability-and-cost problem

In a capacity- C initialized model array, each byte independently equals zero with probability p and nonzero otherwise. A bounded scalar scan stops at zero or capacity. Derive the probability of success and expected number of byte reads for 0<p≤1.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Failure means all C bytes are nonzero, so success probability is 1−(1−p)C. Read number j+1 occurs precisely when the first j bytes are nonzero, for 0≤j<C. By indicator summation, expected reads are ∑j=0C−1(1−p)j=[1−(1−p)C]/p. This includes failure paths reading the whole range. For p=1 and positive capacity, exactly one read occurs. For zero capacity, both success and read count are zero. This probabilistic initialized model does not justify scanning real uninitialized storage.

Question 56. All suffix lengths without rescanning

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original algorithm-design problem

Given one valid string of length n, produce the lengths of all suffixes in linear time. Compare with independently calling a scalar strlen at every suffix.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

First scan once to obtain n. For each k=0,…,n, output n−k. The scan takes n+1 byte tests and there are n+1 arithmetic outputs, so total time is linear. Independently scanning every suffix uses (n+1)(n+2)/2 byte tests. The optimization is valid because each suffix shares the same terminator and no mutation changes it during output. If another operation inserts a zero or modifies termination midway, the cached relationship must be reconsidered. The result reuses a proved representation invariant rather than caching an unexplained guess.

Question 57. Deleting a whole interval

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original generalized movement formula

A length- n string loses content indices p through p+r−1, with 0≤p≤n and 0≤r≤n−p. Derive the movement count and final length, including the case r=0.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The remaining suffix begins at p+r and ends at the original terminator index n, so it contains n−p−r+1 bytes. Move that range to index p using memmove, giving final length n−r. If r=0, source and destination are identical, and the modeled move copies the unchanged suffix; it is valid for memmove but may be skipped as an optimization. If p+r=n, only the terminator moves. Writing an early zero without moving the remaining suffix would truncate the string instead of deleting the selected internal interval.

Question 58. Inserting an entire string

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original generalized capacity proof

A length- n destination receives a disjoint source string of length m at position p≤n. Derive capacity, suffix move count, and total written bytes for a direct insertion using memmove then memcpy of content only.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Final content length is n+m, so capacity must be at least n+m+1, checked without overflow. The old suffix from p through zero contains n−p+1 bytes and moves right by m. Copy the m inserted content bytes into the gap without its terminator, because a zero there would hide the moved suffix. Total direct writes are n−p+1+m. The insertion source must remain unchanged by moving the destination; the disjoint-source assumption guarantees that. For m=0, the operation may be skipped. Aliased insertion needs separate saved-source reasoning.

Question 59. Aliased insertion source

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original advanced alias counterexample

Why is it unsafe to assume the preceding insertion algorithm works unchanged when its source pointer points into the destination? Use "abcd", source s+2, and insertion at index 0 to explain the dependency.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The intended inserted source value is the original suffix cd, so the desired final string is cdabcd. Moving the whole destination right by two first changes bytes at the original source positions 2 and 3: they now contain a and b. Reading s+2 afterward therefore copies ab, not the intended original cd. Each individual move can be within capacity and still violate the algorithm's source-value invariant. Save the source bytes independently before movement or derive a special overlap-safe method that preserves their original positions. Capacity alone does not solve aliasing.

Question 60. Replacing a substring with a different length

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original formula synthesis

A length- n string replaces r content bytes at position p by m disjoint content bytes. Derive final length, capacity, and trailing move count. State necessary index constraints.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Require 0≤p≤n and 0≤r≤n−p. The preserved suffix begins at p+r and includes n−p−r+1 bytes through zero. Move it to p+m, then write the m replacement bytes into the gap. Final length is n−r+m and capacity must exceed that length. Compute n-r only after validating r≤n, then validate addition against available capacity rather than allowing unsigned wrap. Expansion and contraction differ only in move direction, handled by memmove. The replacement source must survive the movement unchanged.

Question 61. An idiomatic copy expression

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original sequencing and count problem

Under valid writable disjoint ranges, analyze while ((*d++ = *s++) != '\0') { } for source length n. What are the final pointer offsets, assignments, and body iterations?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each condition evaluation reads one source byte, assigns it to the current destination, and advances both pointers. The assignment expression's value is then compared with zero. There are n+1 assignments including the terminator and n empty-body iterations. Both pointers finish at offset n+1 from their initial positions, one past the copied representation. This is valid because d and s are distinct pointer variables and the source/destination objects satisfy the copy preconditions. Save the original destination if the interface must return its starting pointer rather than the advanced cursor.

Question 62. Precedence does not solve sequencing

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original C17 undefined-expression problem

Is s[i] = s[i++]; a valid way to copy a byte to itself and advance i in C17? Explain why a precedence tree is insufficient, and give a sequenced alternative.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The expression modifies i through postfix increment while another evaluation uses i to determine the left-hand subscript without the sequencing needed by C17. The unsequenced modification and value computation make the behavior undefined. Operator precedence determines grouping but does not add a sequencing relationship between these evaluations. If the intention is a harmless self-assignment followed by advancement, write s[i]=s[i]; ++i; as separate full expressions, or simply increment when the assignment is unnecessary. The valid copy idiom with distinct source and destination cursor variables has a different dependence structure.

Question 63. Returning different kinds of storage

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

MIT-inspired independently reconstructed lifetime problem

Classify functions returning a pointer to a local char a[], a static char a[], a string literal, and a caller-supplied array. Discuss lifetime and permission to modify separately.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

An automatic local array ceases to exist on return, so a returned pointer cannot be used afterward. A static array survives for the program's lifetime and can be mutable, but repeated calls share its state. A literal also has static lifetime but must not be modified. A caller-supplied array survives only as long as the caller keeps its object alive; mutability depends on the actual object and interface. A pointer return alone does not transfer ownership or allocate a fresh copy. Correct contracts describe lifetime, sharing, mutability, and who may free storage independently.

Question 64. Constness and changing a view

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original pointer-contract problem

For char a[]="cat"; const char *p=a; char *q=a;, classify p++, *p='b', q[0]='b', and p=q. Does const char *p guarantee that observed content cannot change?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The pointer p itself is not const, so it may advance within the array's pointer domain and may be assigned q. Writing through *p violates the const-qualified lvalue constraint and requires a diagnostic. Writing through q is allowed because the underlying array is mutable, and the bytes observed by aliases can therefore change. If p was advanced, its view also begins at a different position. Use char * const p to make a pointer variable nonassignable, and const char * const p to apply both restrictions through that declaration. Neither qualifier alone proves exclusive ownership.

Question 65. A finite byte alphabet and character classes

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original table-index problem

A frequency algorithm uses size_t freq[256]={0}; ++freq[s[i]];. State the two independent assumptions it needs, and repair it for a stated eight-bit byte model.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It needs byte values to lie within 0 through 255 and the subscript to be nonnegative. Eight-bit bytes supply the range only after interpreting the stored byte as unsigned; signed plain char can still produce a negative index. Under the explicitly stated eight-bit model, write ++freq[(unsigned char)s[i]]. For a general C implementation, CHAR_BIT may exceed eight and a 256-entry table is insufficient. Also decide whether zero terminates the traversal or is counted as raw binary data. The table shape follows the representation's universe, not a visual notion of characters.

Question 66. First mismatch distributions

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original probability-and-comparison derivation

Two independent fixed-length strings of length n use an alphabet of q≥2 nonzero bytes uniformly. A scalar comparison stops at the first differing pair, or compares the terminating zeros if equal. Derive expected byte-pair comparisons.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Pair index j is inspected if all j preceding content pairs agree. For each pair, agreement probability is 1/q, independently, so survival probability is q−j. Indices run from 0 through n, where index n is the equal zero pair when all content agrees. By indicator summation, expectation is ∑j=0nq−j=(1−q−(n+1))/(1−1/q). The worst case remains n+1, even though the expectation approaches q/(q−1). The model assumes fixed equal lengths and independent uniformly selected symbols; it does not describe arbitrary natural-language text.

Question 67. Counting constrained values in a buffer

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original combinatorial synthesis

A capacity-7 buffer uses an alphabet of four nonzero symbols, one marked x. How many representable length-6 string values contain exactly two x symbols? How many complete arrays correspond to each such value?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Choose the two marked positions in (62)=15 ways. Each of the other four positions uses one of three unmarked symbols, giving 15·34=1215 values. Because length 6 uses all six content slots and the last slot for zero, no positions remain after termination; each value has exactly one complete array representation under this alphabet-plus-zero model. For a shorter length, unused suffix positions would create multiple storage states. The marked symbol x is content, not the sentinel; replacing it by an actual zero byte would change the representation problem.

Question 68. Maximum naive comparison work over pattern length

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original optimization problem

For a fixed text length n≥1, the naive worst-case comparison formula is f(m)=m(n−m+1) for 1≤m≤n. Determine the maximum over integer m.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Complete the square: f(m)=(n+1)2/4−(m−(n+1)/2)2. It is maximized by the integer or integers closest to (n+1)/2, giving ⌊(n+1)2/4⌋. Both nearest integers are valid for the specified range. A worst-case input can be constructed separately for each chosen length using an all-a text and a pattern ending in b. A long pattern has more comparisons per alignment but fewer alignments; the optimum balances the two rather than always taking m=n.

Question 69. The last zero after mutation

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original view-changing problem

Start with char s[8]="abcdef";. Execute s[2]=0; s[4]='X';. Determine strlen(s), strlen(s+3), and the final stored bytes. Does the second write change the first string value?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Initialization stores a b c d e f 0 0. The writes produce a b 0 d X f 0 0. From the base, the first zero is at 2, so length is 2 and value is ab. From index 3, the suffix is dXf, length 3. The second write modifies storage after the first view's terminator, so it does not change that view's value, although it changes the suffix view. Both writes lie within a mutable array. A single object can support several views with distinct visible content.

Question 70. Appending to a suffix view

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original pointer-and-capacity synthesis

An array of capacity 12 holds "abcdef". A writable view begins at p=s+2. What are the view's length and remaining capacity? Does appending "XYZ" through p fit, and what is the full base string afterward?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The view's content is cdef, length 4, and its accessible remaining capacity is 12−2=10. Appending three bytes requires 4+3+1=8 bytes in that view and fits. The append overwrites the original zero at base index 6 with X, then stores Y, Z, and zero at indices 7, 8, and 9. The full base string becomes abcdefXYZ, length 9. The capacity supplied for the view must be reduced by its offset; carrying the full base capacity would overstate its writable extent.

Question 71. Copying the empty string

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original minimum-object problem

What is the smallest destination capacity for copying "" with strcpy? Contrast a one-byte writable array, a zero-capacity custom checked request, and a null destination.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The empty source contains no content but still contains one stored zero, so a whole-string copy requires capacity 1. A one-byte writable destination receives zero and becomes a valid empty string. A custom checked copy with capacity zero rejects because source length 0 is not less than capacity 0. Passing a null destination to strcpy violates its contract even for an empty source because the terminator must be written. This boundary case exposes the error in formulas that reserve no storage for an empty value.

Copying an empty string writes one zero

Every displayed byte belongs to a fixed array slot. Green NUL cells are zero bytes; the first zero defines each string view. Counters exclude preflight validation scans.

Initial byte objects. Zero marks a terminator; later bytes remain visible.

Step 1 of 3

r=0,w=0,c=0

Question 72. Zero append limit versus missing destination terminator

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original precondition problem

Does strncat(d,s,0) repair a destination array that contains no zero within its extent? Explain why the source limit does not remove the destination's string precondition.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The function must locate the end of the destination string before appending its terminating zero. A source limit of zero prevents appending source content, but the destination still must already designate a valid string. Without an in-bounds terminator, scanning for its end violates the object bound. Thus the call is invalid; it is not a bounded destination validator. To establish an empty destination, write d[0]=0 only after proving positive writable capacity. For a valid destination, a zero limit leaves its value unchanged but still operates under the interface's pointer requirements.

Question 73. Course-inspired halving-index copy

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Princeton-inspired independently reconstructed debugging synthesis

A function copies source positions ⌊n/2⌋,⌊n/4⌋,… until the index becomes zero. For "abcdefghijklmnop", determine output, copied count, and capacity. State the key repairs to a version using uninitialized destination index, sizeof on pointer parameters, and strlen(s) before a null check.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Length is 16, and indices are 8, 4, 2, 1. Zero-based source bytes are i, e, c, b, so the output is iecb. It needs four content bytes plus zero, capacity 5. Initialize the destination index to zero, carry destination capacity explicitly instead of comparing pointer sizes, and test a permitted null source before calling strlen. Write a final terminator unless the contract explicitly guarantees untouched zero-filled storage. For general n≥1, the copied count is ⌊log2n⌋; empty input copies nothing. Use size_t for lengths rather than narrowing into int.

Question 74. Lowercase counting without encoding shortcuts

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Cambridge-inspired independently reconstructed counting task

Design a single-pass lowercase counter for a valid string. State its invariant, classification-domain conversion, complexity, and why the ASCII test 'a'<=c && c<='z' needs an encoding assumption.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Initialize a size_t counter to zero; scan each nonzero byte once and increment when islower((unsigned char)s[i]) is nonzero. The invariant is that the count equals the number of classified lowercase bytes in the processed prefix. At termination the prefix is the entire string, proving the result. The loop takes Θ(n+1) time and constant additional space. The cast supplies the required classification domain, while locale determines lowercase membership. A contiguous-letter range test assumes an encoding with that range property; C guarantees digit contiguity but not one universal contiguous lowercase range.

Question 75. A valid bounded prefix need not be a string

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original interface distinction

Two readable arrays each have exactly three initialized nonzero bytes. Can strncmp(a,b,3) be valid when strcmp(a,b) is not? Explain the required accessible range and stopping behavior.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Yes. strncmp compares no more than three bytes and does not need a terminator beyond them if all three positions are readable. It can compare those bounded arrays and return based on the first mismatch or equality over all three. strcmp requires complete terminated strings and, if no earlier mismatch establishes a result in a particular implementation, cannot be justified by these unterminated objects; the string precondition is absent. A valid bounded prefix interface and a valid whole-string interface carry different contracts. Both still require valid pointer values and appropriate readable bytes.

Question 76. An overlap check itself needs a domain

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original advanced pointer-contract problem

A programmer attempts to detect arbitrary pointer-range overlap with if(dst<src+count && src<dst+count). Why is this not a universally portable check for unrelated C objects? How can an interface avoid the problem?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Relational pointer comparisons and pointer arithmetic have object-domain restrictions. Forming src+count requires that the offset stay within its array or one-past, and relational ordering between unrelated objects is not a general portable total-address comparison. A formula valid for integer intervals in a flat model does not automatically become valid C pointer code. One design accepts a single array base, its capacity, and validated integer offsets; then both ranges are described within one object. Another states nonoverlap as a caller precondition or simply uses memmove for a valid requested move.

Question 77. Storage states conditioned on length

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original combinatorial ratio

A capacity- C array uses zero plus q≥1 nonzero byte values. For a fixed length j<C, determine the number of complete states and the number of states per abstract value. Specialize to C=6,q=3,j=2.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first j bytes are nonzero, giving qj choices; the next byte is fixed zero; the final C−j−1 bytes have (q+1)C−j−1 choices. Total states are qj(q+1)C−j−1, and each of the qj abstract values has (q+1)C−j−1 representations. For the specialization, there are 32·43=576 states and 64 states per value. The multiplication counts independent storage positions. It does not treat padding variants as different visible strings.

Question 78. Concatenation versus raw copying

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original embedded-zero synthesis

Let char s[]="ab\0cd"; and let a large zero-initialized destination begin with "X". Compare appending with strcat(d,s) and copying all six source bytes to d+1 with memcpy. What does the destination print as a string in each case?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

strcat sees source length 2 and appends a b 0, so the destination's visible value is Xab. Copying all six source bytes stores a b 0 c d 0 after X, preserving the source's hidden suffix too. The destination still prints as Xab because its first zero is at index 3. Equal printed values do not imply equal copied byte regions. The raw copy's count comes from the source array extent, while the append count comes from its string view. Both operations require sufficient disjoint valid storage.

Question 79. A proof of bounded matching safety

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original invariant synthesis

For the displayed naive matcher with 0<m≤n, prove every read t[i+j] stays inside the text content and every candidate start is considered at most once. What changes for finding all overlapping matches?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The outer loop establishes 0≤i≤n−m; the inner loop establishes 0≤j<m. Hence i+j≤n−m+m−1=n−1, so each text content read is in range; pattern indices are likewise below m. Increasing i by one visits each feasible start in increasing order exactly once. For first-match search, the outer invariant excludes all smaller positions before a return. To find all overlapping matches, record success and continue with i+1 instead of returning. Skipping ahead by m would adopt a different nonoverlap policy and miss valid starts.

Question 80. Combined capacity, mutation, and cost audit

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original final synthesis

A capacity-10 array begins with "orbit". Append "XY", delete content indices 1 and 2, then reverse the remaining content. Derive every intermediate length and value, each direct move/write count, and the final terminator index.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Initial length is 5. Appending two bytes requires eight storage bytes and fits capacity 10; it writes X, Y, zero, giving orbitXY of length 7. Deleting positions 1 and 2 removes r and b; the suffix beginning at old index 3 contains i t X Y 0, five moved bytes, yielding oitXY of length 5. Reversal swaps positions (0,4) and (1,3), producing YXtio. The terminator remains at index 5. Under the displayed three-assignment swap, reversal has two swaps and six assignments; count its length scan separately. Unused capacity never participates in reversal.

Append XY after orbit and move the terminator

Every displayed byte belongs to a fixed array slot. Green NUL cells are zero bytes; the first zero defines each string view. Counters exclude preflight validation scans.

Initial byte objects. Zero marks a terminator; later bytes remain visible.

26. Examination rules and advanced pitfalls

Rule 1

One array, three string views. Determine the first terminator relative to the given starting address; capacity and total zero count do not determine that view's length.

Rule 2

Exact-size initialization. Separate initialization constraints from the later library contract; a valid declaration can create a nonstring array.

Rule 3

Embedded escape and size. Expand escapes, retain explicit embedded zeros, and then add the literal's implicit final zero before counting storage.

Rule 4

Suffix identity and one-past. The empty-string pointer designates the terminator itself; a pointer one past the complete array does not.

Rule 5

Array size inside a function. Array parameter syntax does not transmit the array extent; pass capacity before array-to-pointer conversion loses that information.

Rule 6

Two pointers and an independent copy. Draw object identity before tracing mutation; pointer assignment preserves aliasing, whereas a disjoint byte copy creates separate content storage.

Rule 7

Equal content and unequal objects. Use a string comparison for string equality; equal literal spelling does not establish a required object identity.

Rule 8

Bounded scan failure. A bounded scan returning its bound means no terminator was found; represent that status separately from a successful length.

Rule 9

Short-circuit order. Put the range guard before the indexed access in a short-circuit conjunction; the guard must be established before the read occurs.

Rule 10

Exact scalar length cost. Include the final failing sentinel test and sum repeated suffix costs instead of counting distinct stored bytes only.

Rule 11

A copy that just fits. For a nontruncating string copy, require source length strictly less than destination capacity and retain the terminator in the write count.

Rule 12

Bounded copy padding. When the source ends before the strncpy bound, count zero padding through the entire bound and preserve bytes beyond it.

Rule 13

Bounded copy without a terminator. A strncpy bound limits writes but does not guarantee termination; inspect the resulting complete accessible array before using string functions.

Rule 14

Forced termination and zero capacity. Guard positive capacity before subtracting one, and separate guaranteed termination from a guarantee that no content was truncated.

Rule 15

The exact append bound. Compute append space as capacity minus current length minus one; a strncat bound limits new content, not total storage.

Rule 16

Short source and a large bound. Use the actual minimum of source length and append limit when both are known; a worst-case sufficient bound need not be necessary.

Rule 17

Safe arithmetic without forming an overflowing sum. Establish the existing terminator lies within capacity before using subtraction to validate an append.

Rule 18

Right-overlap propagation. Distinguish a defined faulty handwritten algorithm from an undefined overlapping library call; use original-source semantics for memmove.

Rule 19

Left-overlap movement. An overlapping left shift can copy forward, but the moved range must include the original terminator when moving a whole suffix.

Rule 20

Insertion at all boundary positions. For one nonzero insertion at position p, move n−p+1 bytes, reserve n+2 storage bytes, and count the insertion separately.

Rule 21

Deletion count includes zero. Delete by moving the following suffix through its terminator; omitting zero often duplicates the old last character.

Rule 22

Lexicographic comparison count. Find the first mismatch before considering length; only the sign of a standard string-comparison return is portable.

Rule 23

A proper prefix compares smaller. A comparison bound ending at a common prefix can hide the terminator mismatch that distinguishes complete strings.

Rule 24

Unsigned byte order. Standard string ordering uses unsigned character values; signed plain-char arithmetic is not a substitute.

Rule 25

Equal strings and different storage. String equality ignores bytes after the first zero; fixed-count memory equality does not.

Rule 26

Searching for the terminator. Character search includes the terminating zero, but a failed search returns null and cannot be converted into an offset by subtraction.

Rule 27

Spans are initial segments. Span functions measure a maximal qualifying prefix; set membership is different from a full-string frequency count.

Rule 28

Overlapping substring occurrences. State whether matching returns the first hit, permits overlaps, or advances past a full hit before counting occurrences or work.

Rule 29

Empty and longer patterns. Resolve empty-pattern semantics and rule out a longer pattern before forming an unsigned candidate-range difference.

Rule 30

A tight naive-search worst case. To prove a matching worst case is tight, construct inputs that force the maximum comparisons at every feasible alignment.

Rule 31

A matcher that misses the last start. The last feasible substring start is inclusive; derive it from the last indexed character of the candidate.

Rule 32

Reversal never swaps the terminator. Reverse only the content interval and leave the terminator fixed; an odd-length middle byte needs no swap.

Rule 33

Empty reversal and unsigned indices. An expression inside a skipped body is not evaluated; verify guard placement before classifying unsigned-underflow consequences.

Rule 34

Palindrome comparisons. Distinguish pair comparisons, individual byte observations, and distinct memory locations when deriving exact counts.

Rule 35

Filtering with retained-order proof. For stable compaction, preserve the retained subsequence behind the read head and write a fresh terminator after the last retained byte.

Rule 36

All removed, none removed. Count the operations actually present in the algorithm, including self-writes and final termination, even when the string value is unchanged.

Rule 37

Why repeated deletion is quadratic. Sum suffix lengths for repeated shifting; a single retained-subsequence pass avoids revisiting the remaining input.

Rule 38

Token count and empty fields. Choose whether empty fields carry meaning before choosing a tokenizer; delimiter count plus one applies to the preserving policy.

Rule 39

Nested tokenization state. Independent tokenization traversals need independent continuation state; a null argument to strtok does not identify which previous sequence to resume.

Rule 40

Line input at exact capacity. A full fgets buffer without newline may be only a prefix of the line; preserve real data until stream status and policy are resolved.

Rule 41

Removing newline without losing data. Search for the specific delimiter before deleting it; length alone does not establish that the last byte is a newline.

Rule 42

Formatted input width. For %s, reserve an extra byte beyond the width; %c does not supply string termination or the same whitespace handling.

Rule 43

Formatting and would-have length. Interpret a nonnegative snprintf return as the untruncated content length; compare it with capacity and add one when allocating a complete result.

Rule 44

The special zero-size formatting query. Zero work does not automatically permit invalid pointers; rely on the particular interface's explicit null-pointer exception.

Rule 45

Character classification domain. Convert stored plain-char bytes into the classification domain before the call, and keep stream EOF distinct from character data.

Rule 46

Numeric conversion needs a status. Distinguish a valid zero, no conversion, trailing data, and range failure using the end pointer and error status.

Rule 47

UTF-8 bytes and displayed characters. Keep byte length, code-point count, and grapheme count separate; a correct byte transformation can still be an incorrect human-text transformation.

Rule 48

Rows versus pointer tables. A table's pointer storage does not include its referenced character arrays, and equal total sizes do not imply equal representations or assignment rules.

Rule 49

Arguments and their final sentinel. An argument-list sentinel is a null pointer, while an empty argument is a non-null pointer to a terminating character.

Rule 50

Quadratic repeated concatenation. Account for the increasing existing prefix at every append; enough capacity does not prevent quadratic rescanning.

Rule 51

Geometric buffer growth. A linear sum of geometric growth copies supports amortized cost, not a constant worst-case guarantee for each individual append.

Rule 52

Reallocation and ownership. Preserve the original owner until positive-size reallocation succeeds, then replace old aliases using the new allocation's pointer.

Rule 53

Count abstract string values. For capacity C, sum alphabet powers over content lengths zero through C−1, rather than assigning all slots to content.

Rule 54

Count terminated storage states. For complete storage states, account for arbitrary bytes after the first zero; abstract string counts deliberately identify those states as the same value.

Rule 55

Probability of finding a terminator. Use survival probabilities to count expected scan work, and distinguish a probabilistic initialized model from invalid uninitialized program data.

Rule 56

All suffix lengths without rescanning. Exploit a shared immutable terminator to derive suffix lengths arithmetically after one scan.

Rule 57

Deleting a whole interval. For interval deletion, move the surviving suffix through zero and reduce content length by the deleted interval length.

Rule 58

Inserting an entire string. Move the destination suffix including zero, but copy only inserted content into the gap so that the trailing suffix stays visible.

Rule 59

Aliased insertion source. An internal source can change when the destination shifts; preserve the original source value before applying a disjoint-source insertion algorithm.

Rule 60

Replacing a substring with a different length. Replacement length is old length minus removed content plus inserted content; preserve the entire trailing suffix including termination.

Rule 61

An idiomatic copy expression. In a sentinel-copy idiom, the terminating condition still performs the final assignment and both pointer increments.

Rule 62

Precedence does not solve sequencing. Check sequencing dependencies separately from precedence; a syntactically grouped expression can still contain unsequenced access and modification.

Rule 63

Returning different kinds of storage. Persistent lifetime does not imply writable or independently owned text; state all three properties in a string-returning interface.

Rule 64

Constness and changing a view. Const-qualified pointed-to access and a const pointer variable are separate restrictions; other writable aliases may still change a mutable object.

Rule 65

A finite byte alphabet and character classes. Validate both the byte universe and subscript signedness before using a byte-indexed lookup table.

Rule 66

First mismatch distributions. Expected first-mismatch work follows common-prefix survival probabilities, while equal strings still realize the linear worst case.

Rule 67

Counting constrained values in a buffer. Apply constrained sequence counting only to nonzero content positions, then account separately for the terminator and unused storage.

Rule 68

Maximum naive comparison work over pattern length. When pattern length varies, maximize both factors together; the number of alignments decreases as comparison depth increases.

Rule 69

The last zero after mutation. Mutation after one view's terminator may still change another view that starts later in the same array.

Rule 70

Appending to a suffix view. An interior string view inherits the remaining array extent, not the entire base capacity, and appending through it can extend the base view too.

Rule 71

Copying the empty string. The empty string requires one writable storage byte for copying; zero content length does not mean zero representation size.

Rule 72

Zero append limit versus missing destination terminator. An append limit constrains source content, not the search for the existing destination terminator.

Rule 73

Course-inspired halving-index copy. Debug a string routine by separating pointer validity, capacity, initialized indices, and termination from the intended indexing recurrence.

Rule 74

Lowercase counting without encoding shortcuts. State the character-class policy and argument domain; a familiar alphabetic range is not a language-independent classification guarantee.

Rule 75

A valid bounded prefix need not be a string. Bounded comparison can operate on a sufficiently readable nonterminated prefix; whole-string comparison requires string objects.

Rule 76

An overlap check itself needs a domain. Prove the domain of an overlap test itself; flat numerical address reasoning does not authorize arbitrary C pointer ordering.

Rule 77

Storage states conditioned on length. Conditioning on first-zero position fixes termination but leaves the suffix unrestricted; factor visible value choices from hidden storage choices.

Rule 78

Concatenation versus raw copying. Embedded zeros separate byte-region copying from string concatenation even when the visible output happens to agree.

Rule 79

A proof of bounded matching safety. Combine outer and inner index bounds to prove memory safety, then state the post-match advance policy independently.

Rule 80

Combined capacity, mutation, and cost audit. Recompute the logical length and terminator after each mutation, and derive movement counts from the current representation rather than the original one.

27. Editable memory laboratory

The laboratory executes explicitly specified byte algorithms, not arbitrary C source. Enter printable ASCII strings; \0 inserts a zero byte. Capacity is an actual displayed array extent. It rejects invalid inputs before replacing a valid trace. Cells remain at their indices while the read/write heads move. “Reject” is the model's checked outcome, not an attempt to simulate undefined behavior. Stored zero bytes beyond the first terminator remain visible.

Use at most fifteen entered printable ASCII bytes; \0 inserts an embedded zero. A final source zero is added automatically. Destination capacity is between one and sixteen bytes. Only the selected operation's parameters apply. All traces start paused. Invalid inputs preserve the preceding valid result. Scan examines the displayed source extent; capacity controls the destination object. The laboratory's zero-filled unused destination cells are initialized model data, never a claim that automatic C arrays initialize themselves.
